Hi Alice — below are precise examples and the billing rules we apply. I kept the math explicit so you can plug in your committed rates.

High-level rules (short):
- All model-visible context (system + user + assistant history + any tool results that are fed back into the model) are billed as input tokens.
- Tokens the model emits as generated text are billed as output tokens.
- When a tool is invoked and returns content that is subsequently consumed by the model, that returned content is counted as input on the next model call (not as model output).
- Rounding is applied at the API-call level (post-batching). We do NOT round per-stream-chunk. For streaming, we measure the full output token count produced by the model for that single API call and round that once.

Worked examples (explicit):
Example A — system + user prompt
- System prompt: 3000 tokens (long system instructions)
- User message: 200 tokens
- No prior assistant messages, single call to generate reply
Billing: Input tokens = 3000 + 200 = 3200; Output tokens = tokens generated by the model (see below). If your request results in a 150-token reply, you'd be charged 3200 input + 150 output (rounded according to call-level policy).

Example B — tool call that returns KB text + assistant reply
Flow: Client issues a user prompt (100 tokens) -> model decides to call KB lookup tool -> Redwood forwards parameters to the KB (tool invocation metadata not billed as model tokens) -> KB returns 800-token snippet -> model ingests snippet and generates 150-token assistant reply that is streamed back to the client.
How we count:
- The 100-token user prompt is input.
- The 800-token KB snippet is not billed as model output; instead, because the model receives that 800-token blob as part of its context for the subsequent model call, we count the 800 tokens as input on that model call. 
- The model-generated 150-token assistant text is billed as output.
So billed tokens (single end-to-end interaction): Input = 100 + 800 = 900; Output = 150.
Note: any tokens produced internally by the tool system (e.g., tool metadata) are not counted as model tokens unless the model actually sees them as text in a subsequent call.

Example C — streaming partials and rounding
Scenario: Model produces 2 chunks streamed to the client: chunk1 = 40 tokens, chunk2 = 60 tokens; total = 100 tokens produced by the model for that API call.
Billing: We take the full output token total for that API call (100 tokens) and apply rounding once. In practice we truncate token math to whole tokens (tokens are integer counts) and then do any rate-tier rounding/pack rounding at the call aggregation step. We do NOT round 40 -> 1, 60 -> 1 and charge 2 tokens; we charge the actual 100 tokens (rounded once per call) at your output unit rate.

Edge-case: continuous batching
When requests are continuously batched by our serving layer, we attribute tokens back to the originating customer request. Rounding still happens per logical API call once tokens are attributed — batching does not create additional per-customer rounding noise beyond the single-call rounding.

Short answers to your numbered list:
1) Yes — system (3k) + user (200) are input tokens.
2) Tool-returned KB content is counted as input on the model call that consumes it; the 800-token KB text itself is not billed as model output. The model's reply is billed as output.
3) Rounding is per API call (post-stream), not per stream chunk.

If you'd like, we can provide the same examples with your committed tier rates plugged in to produce an estimated invoice line for a month of X queries.

— Karthik
Director, Pricing & Billing (Redwood Inference)

Alice — quick answers and next steps from Sales Ops side: 

1) How you present the KB text in the request matters only insofar as what the model actually "sees" as context. If you attach a tool_result as an assistant/tool message and the model consumes it directly, those tokens are input. If you merge the snippet into the user message before the call, it's still input. Practically, there's no difference in billing: token attribution follows what the model ingests, not the envelope field name.

2) Committed discounts and pooling: when you're on a committed token bucket, we apply discounts at the billing aggregation level (monthly). Rounding is still performed per API call for attribution, but the effective unit price applied during invoice consolidation respects your committed tier. In other words: rounding rules don't change, but your per-token price does once committed tiers are applied on the invoice.

3) Next step: I've attached a one-page worked-out estimate for ACME at 250k queries/month using Karthik's examples and your committed tier assumptions (see attached link). If that looks good, we can lock a time on 7/16 10:30am PT to walk through the numbers live.

Thanks — Monica
